# Hard-to-vary report: *The Time Machine*, chs. I–VI (excerpt)

## 1. The question, frozen

The document (title and opening both point here) is built around one claim: **a machine can carry a person through time**, and the craft question it raises is *why does the reader come to accept that, at least provisionally, rather than dismiss it as a parlour trick?* Domain: creative choices (this tests whether choices do a job, not whether they are fine writing). Range: this excerpt only, ending mid-sentence in ch. VI. I am not testing the separate "sunset of mankind" theme (decayed buildings, frail Eloi) — that answers a different question (what has happened to progress) and is set aside as borrowed, not idle.

## 2. The explanation in parts

- **A. The Fourth-Dimension speech** — jargon-with-specifics, challenged point by point by Filby.
- **B. A panel of distinct skeptics** — Filby (common sense), Medical Man (physical objection: up/down freedom), Psychologist (explains things away), Provincial Mayor (vague credulity).
- **C. Multi-angle model demonstration** — narrator, Filby, Medical Man, Provincial Mayor, Psychologist all watching from different sides as the model vanishes.
- **D. The Psychologist's on-the-spot patch** ("presentation below the threshold") for why a past-bound machine wasn't seen in the room before.
- **E. The unfinished full-size machine** shown in the workshop.
- **F. The week-later return** — dirty, wounded, starving, torn bloody socks.
- **G. Persistent mockery** (Editor, Journalist) even after F.
- **H. The sensory ride itself** — day/night flicker, seasons blurring, landscape melting.
- **I. The stated risk of materialising inside solid matter.**

## 3. Part by part

| Part | Mark | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A, specific 4-D content | Loose | Swap for ether-vibration jargon, keep Filby's pushback: same effect. What survives — confident talk met by a named objection — is the real part, not the physics. |
| A, "jargon + named pushback" | Held | Remove it (just assert time travel works) and the respectability job fails; nothing else does it. |
| B, four *distinct* objections | Held | Cut the Medical Man's up/down point and that axis goes untested — no one else covers it. Coverage of separate doubts is the job. |
| B, Filby's red hair | Idle | Swap for anything; nothing depends on it. |
| C, multiple vantage points | Held | With one witness a reader can suspect an angle-dependent trick; front/back/both-profile coverage closes that route. |
| D, "below the threshold" patch | Held if | Held only by the job "survive the visibility objection" — a job the narrator himself raises, and the text flags as glib (later called "wooden"). No gauge is offered, so it is a catch-all kept alive only if meant to read as thin. |
| F, specific injuries (dirt, cut chin, torn socks) | Loose | Swap for sunburn and fatigue: still works. |
| F, visible bodily cost, independent of his say-so | Held | Remove it (he just reports a trip) and the shift from ridicule to attention loses its warrant. The single most load-bearing part here. |
| G, mockery persisting after F | Held | Add a job: must a skeptic be answered, not just outlasted? Text never converts Filby/Editor here — realistic testimony isn't universally believed, ruling out the too-easy rival where evidence convinces everyone at once. |
| H, exact images (rhododendrons, hail colour) | Loose | Swap for other blurring-season imagery; no loss. |
| H, continuous escalating sensation | Held | Remove it and time travel is pure assertion again; this is what makes ch. IV read as experience. |
| I, danger of materialising inside matter | Held (2 jobs) | Gives the crash a mechanical cause, and explains why stopping, unlike starting, is abrupt. Remove it: the crash has no reason. |
| E, the unfinished full machine | Held if | Held only if "a tabletop trick needs a costlier research context to be credible" is a real requirement — plausible for the era, but I am adding that job; the text doesn't argue it. |

## 4. Whole-explanation checks

**Flip.** Had the Time Traveller returned clean, calm, and merely telling a nice story, would A–C and E still carry belief on their own? No — the excerpt leans on F for the emotional turn from mockery to attention. So the parts do not cover every outcome equally, which is a good sign, not a weakness.

**Reverse.** Does the reader's half-belief track the evidence given (poke the cause, effect moves), or is it partly primed beforehand by genre — a book titled *The Time Machine*, bought expecting time travel to be real within it? Some of the persuasive work here is plausibly borrowed from that offstage convention rather than supplied by the text itself; I can't settle this from the document alone, so I mark it unknown rather than held.

**Build the best rival.** A version that opens in medias res with F and H, then flashes back, cutting A–D and the model demonstration entirely, could plausibly do the "reader accepts the premise" job just as well (many later time-travel stories work this way). If so, A–D are not strictly necessary for bare credibility; they are held only for a narrower, added job — that the persuasion must also look scientifically respectable to a skeptical contemporary audience, and stay in the register of a gentlemen's dinner-table argument rather than pure spectacle. I have not tested that narrower job against a rival version; it is recorded as open.

**Catch-all check.** D is the one clear catch-all ("diluted presentation" can absorb any awkward non-appearance). It has no stated gauge. That the narration itself treats it skeptically (calling the account "wooden") suggests Wells is using it as characterisation of the Psychologist's glibness, not as a serious patch — which would make it Borrowed from the "gullible listener" thread rather than load-bearing for the main claim. Flagged, not resolved.

## 5. What would make it harder to vary

- Give D a gauge: some detail the characters could check (a mark on the wall, a servant's testimony) that would show whether "presentation below threshold" is really happening, rather than leaving it a bare assertion.
- Test the genre-priming worry directly: compare this credibility structure against a version presented with no title or foreknowledge, to see how much work A–E do once genre expectation is subtracted.

## 6. What this does not show

Hard to vary is not a verdict on literary quality, on Wells's science, or on whether time travel is "really" plausible. It shows which choices are doing identifiable work in this excerpt and which are decoration, nothing more. It also says nothing about the decline/Eloi material, which answers a different question.

## 7. One next step

Test Part F against its nearest rival directly: find a passage elsewhere in the book (or draft one) where the Time Traveller returns with a *told* but not *shown* cost, and see whether the audience's shift from mockery still lands — that would confirm or break F's "held" mark.
